What makes London mixed-use different

A mixed-use scheme in London is not two projects stacked. Residential and commercial uses have different fire strategies, different acoustic requirements, different servicing regimes, different lease structures and different planning obligations. When they share a structure they share risks: a compartmentation failure between C3 and A3 uses is a licensing problem and an insurance problem, not just a construction one.

The planning route is also its own project. Section 106 obligations, Community Infrastructure Levy, affordable-housing viability, active-frontage requirements and the London Plan's H1/H2 policies all shape the developable envelope. Getting these settled at pre-application is the difference between a 12-week determination and an 18-month refusal at committee.

How we deliver, in order

  1. AppraisalSite walk, desktop planning study, indicative massing, sketch GDV and cost plan against a target IRR.
  2. Planning strategyPre-application with the borough, agreement on unit mix, height, affordable housing, active frontage and s.106 heads of terms.
  3. Design coordinationArchitect, structural, MEP, fire and acoustic engineers brought onto a single coordinated design, BIM to Level 2 where the scheme warrants it.
  4. Tender / procurementTwo-stage tender or negotiated route, priced against the coordinated design not a wishlist.
  5. Enabling worksDemolition, service diversions, hoardings, site set-up and any early temporary works ahead of the main contract.
  6. SuperstructureSubstructure, frame, envelope and roof, with movement monitoring on adjoining structures where required.
  7. Fit-out & servicesCat A base build, residential fit-out, MEP first fix through commissioning, riser coordination and lift installation.
  8. PC, handover & aftercareStatutory sign-offs, warranty pack, letting-agent pack and defects management through the rectification period.

Frequently asked questions

What counts as mixed-use for planning purposes?

Any scheme with two or more principal uses in the same building, most commonly residential over ground-floor commercial. The Use Class Order groups uses, but the London Plan and the relevant borough Local Plan will usually govern the acceptable mix, the required active frontage and any affordable-housing proportion.

Do you take equity or work strictly as a contractor?

We deliver as contractor on a JCT contract, and separately we can co-invest or take part-equity on schemes where the numbers, the sponsor and the exit align. The two roles are kept in separate agreements so the contractor risk and the equity risk are not commingled.

How do you handle phasing around sitting commercial tenants?

Phasing is agreed at planning stage and priced at tender. Typical patterns are top-down (residential above completed first, ground-floor retail refitted last) or bottom-up (retail decanted, redelivered, then upper storeys). Out-of-hours access, protected escape routes and hoarding lines are agreed with each occupier before works start.

How is fire strategy handled between residential and commercial uses?

A named fire engineer produces the fire strategy at RIBA Stage 3 and signs off the as-built condition. Standard requirements include separate protected escape routes, one-hour compartmentation between uses, dedicated smoke control on residential lobbies and independent alarm systems for the two occupancies.

What sits under s.106 vs CIL?

CIL is a fixed borough charge per square metre of new floorspace, published in the borough's CIL charging schedule. Section 106 covers site-specific obligations negotiated with the planning authority: affordable housing, highways works, employment and training, carbon offset and public realm.

What warranties do lenders and buyers expect?

Structural warranties (NHBC, LABC, ICW, BuildZone, CRL) covering the residential element; collateral warranties from the design team and key subcontractors to the funder and to the incoming purchaser or head lessee; and manufacturer warranties on the envelope and roof for the coverage period the lender's monitoring surveyor requires.
